annotations.text: Sparse attention enables efficient long-context inference by routing each query to a subset of key-value buckets, but learned routers require per-head training while training-free alternatives like symmetric k-means achieve limited quality. We investigate whether training-free routing can approach learned router quality. Surprisingly, we find that geometric moment matching—aligning query-key distributions via dot-product-preserving gauge transforms—provides no improvement over symmetric k-means. This reveals that routing quality depends on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass, not on distribution alignment. Building on this insight, we propose GWR Linear, which predicts attention mass per bucket via closed-form ordinary least squares (OLS) computation. On Qwen2.5- 7B, GWR Linear achieves 72.6% attention-mass recall@32, closing 63.6% of the gap between symmetric k-means (51.3%) and a learned MLP router (84.8%) without any iterative training. Gap closure increases with routing budget (44%–80%) and generalizes across attention heads (mean 69.8% across 6 heads spanning layers 2–26).
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the core claim that GWR Linear achieves 72.6% recall@32 via closed-form OLS attention-mass prediction. However, the novelty positioning requires tighter bounding against prior training-free approaches.

**Evidence-grounded diagnosis:** The abstract claims GWR Linear predicts attention mass per bucket via closed-form computation, positioning it as a new insight. Yet Expected Attention (Devoto et al., 2025) already demonstrates that closed-form expected attention scores can be computed for KV pairs by leveraging the distributional properties of LLM activations, without training. Both methods operate training-free and use closed-form statistics on calibration data. The manuscript does not currently differentiate itself from this prior work.

**Why it matters:** Without explicit positioning against Expected Attention, the core novelty of GWR Linear (OLS on bucket-aggregated attention) appears partially overlapping. Reviewers may perceive the contribution as incremental rather than genuinely new.

**Concrete revision plan:** Add one sentence explicitly differentiating GWR Linear from Expected Attention. Expected Attention computes per-KV-pair importance scores for pruning; GWR Linear computes per-bucket scores for routing queries to subsets. These are complementary objectives (pruning vs routing), not identical problems.

Mentor Revised Version: "Building on this insight, we propose GWR Linear, which predicts attention mass per bucket via closed-form ordinary least squares (OLS) computation. Unlike prior closed-form KV importance estimators (Devoto et al., 2025) that score individual tokens for pruning, GWR Linear regresses from query embeddings to bucket-level attention distributions, enabling query-dependent routing without training. On Qwen2.5-7B, GWR Linear achieves 72.6% attention-mass recall@32..."

References:
[1] Expected Attention: KV Cache Compression by Estimating Attention from Future Queries Distribution 2510.00636
annotations.summary: Novelty overlap: Expected Attention (2510.00636) also uses closed-form attention scoring training-free; abstract must differentiate pruning objective from GWR Linear's routing objective.

annotations.text:
1 INTRODUCTION
Long-context inference has become increasingly important for large language models (LLMs) in applications such as document understanding, code analysis, and multi-turn dialogue. However, the quadratic complexity of self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) creates a fundamental bottleneck: as context length grows, attention computation and key-value (KV) cache memory become prohibitively expensive. While hardware-aware implementations like FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023) optimize memory access patterns, they do not reduce the underlying O(n<sup>2</sup>) complexity.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph establishes the long-context inference problem and O(n²) bottleneck, which is a standard opening. The writing is clear but misses an opportunity to foreground the routing challenge early.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Big Picture -> Problem. Sets up the computational bottleneck of full attention.

**Concrete defect:** The paragraph discusses general quadratic complexity but does not connect to the specific bottleneck that routing introduces—namely, that even with sparse attention, memory access patterns and KV cache fetching remain the dominant cost. The current wording implies FlashAttention solves memory access, which is misleading; it optimizes I/O but does not reduce KV cache size.

**Why it matters:** Without clarifying that the bottleneck is KV cache memory access (not just FLOPs), the motivation for sparse attention routing is weakened. Readers may not see why reducing attention computation matters when FlashAttention already handles the I/O efficiently.

**Exact modification action:** Add one sentence connecting sparse attention to the memory-access bottleneck, not just compute.

Mentor Revised Version: "Long-context inference has become increasingly important for large language models (LLMs) in applications such as document understanding, code analysis, and multi-turn dialogue. However, the quadratic complexity of self-attention creates a fundamental bottleneck: as context length grows, both attention computation and key-value (KV) cache memory bandwidth become prohibitively expensive. While hardware-aware implementations like FlashAttention optimize memory access patterns, they do not reduce the underlying O(n²) memory footprint or the fraction of KV cache that must be fetched per query."
annotations.summary: Opening paragraph should connect O(n²) complexity to KV cache memory bandwidth, not just compute, to strengthen motivation for routing-based sparse attention.

annotations.text:
Long-context inference has become increasingly important for large language models (LLMs) in applications such as document understanding, code analysis, and multi-turn dialogue. However, the quadratic complexity of self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) creates a fundamental bottleneck: as context length grows, attention computation and key-value (KV) cache memory become prohibitively expensive. While hardware-aware implementations like FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023) optimize memory access patterns, they do not reduce the underlying O(n<sup>2</sup>) complexity.
Sparse attention offers a promising solution by attending to only a subset of keys for each query. Recent work on inference-time sparse attention (Mazar’e et al., 2025) partitions keys into buckets via clustering and routes each query to a small number of buckets, achieving substantial speedups while maintaining accuracy. The key challenge is routing: determining which buckets contain the most relevant keys for each query. Learned routers achieve high quality but require per-head training, creating deployment barriers. Training-free alternatives like symmetric k-means routing—assigning queries to buckets using the same centroids as keys—are simple but limited in quality due to the distribution mismatch between queries and keys in pretrained models.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph introduces sparse attention and the routing challenge, positioning learned vs. training-free methods. The narrative is clear, but the gap statement needs tightening.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Problem Context -> Gap. Introduces sparse attention routing and contrasts learned routers (high quality, per-head training) with training-free alternatives (simple, limited quality).

**Concrete defect:** The paragraph states that symmetric k-means is "limited in quality due to the distribution mismatch between queries and keys in pretrained models." This is a plausible explanation but is not empirically verified in the manuscript. The paper later shows that geometric alignment (which directly addresses distribution mismatch) provides no improvement. The introduction should foreshadow this counter-intuitive finding more explicitly, as it is central to the paper's main insight.

**Why it matters:** If the introduction simply states distribution mismatch as the problem, readers will naturally expect distribution alignment to be the solution. The actual paper finds alignment is irrelevant. The current setup creates an implicit expectation mismatch between problem framing and actual finding.

**Exact modification action:** Add a sentence that foreshadows the negative result on distribution alignment, creating a cleaner narrative arc.

Mentor Revised Version: "Sparse attention offers a promising solution by attending to only a subset of keys for each query. Recent work on inference-time sparse attention (Mazar'e et al., 2025) partitions keys into buckets via clustering and routes each query to a small number of buckets, achieving substantial speedups while maintaining accuracy. The key challenge is routing: determining which buckets contain the most relevant keys for each query. Learned routers achieve high quality but require per-head training, creating deployment barriers. Training-free alternatives like symmetric k-means routing—assigning queries to buckets using the same centroids as keys—are simple but limited in quality. While the query-key distribution mismatch in pretrained models has been cited as the primary cause, it is unclear whether correcting this mismatch actually improves routing."
annotations.summary: Gap paragraph assumes distribution mismatch is the root cause without foreshadowing the paper's own finding that alignment provides no improvement.

annotations.text:
Sparse attention offers a promising solution by attending to only a subset of keys for each query. Recent work on inference-time sparse attention (Mazar’e et al., 2025) partitions keys into buckets via clustering and routes each query to a small number of buckets, achieving substantial speedups while maintaining accuracy. The key challenge is routing: determining which buckets contain the most relevant keys for each query. Learned routers achieve high quality but require per-head training, creating deployment barriers. Training-free alternatives like symmetric k-means routing—assigning queries to buckets using the same centroids as keys—are simple but limited in quality due to the distribution mismatch between queries and keys in pretrained models.
We investigate whether training-free routing can approach the quality of learned routers. Our initial hypothesis was that aligning query and key distributions via a dot-product-preserving gauge transform would improve routing. Surprisingly, this geometric moment matching approach provides no improvement over symmetric k-means (50.7% vs 51.3% recall). This negative result reveals a key insight: routing quality depends on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass, not on aligning distributions geometrically.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the initial hypothesis (gauge transform alignment) and the surprising negative result. The narrative pivot is well-structured but needs tighter claim bounding.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Negative Result -> Insight. Reports that geometric moment matching provides no improvement and extracts the key insight: routing depends on predicting attention mass, not distribution alignment.

**Concrete defect:** The claim "routing quality depends on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass, not on aligning distributions geometrically" is stated as a definitive conclusion. However, the paper only tests one form of alignment (gauge-coupled ZCA whitening) against one form of prediction (OLS). Stronger alternative alignment methods (e.g., optimal transport, moment matching beyond second order) or other prediction paradigms (e.g., hash-based, kernel-based) are not explored. The causal language ("depends on") is too strong for what is essentially a local empirical observation.

**Why it matters:** If reviewers interpret this as a general statement about routing, they will expect a more comprehensive negative result sweep. Bounding the claim reduces overreach risk.

**Exact modification action:** Soften the causal claim and add scope qualifier.

Mentor Revised Version: "We investigate whether training-free routing can approach the quality of learned routers. Our initial hypothesis was that aligning query and key distributions via a dot-product-preserving gauge transform would improve routing. Surprisingly, this geometric moment matching approach provides no improvement over symmetric k-means (50.7% vs 51.3% recall). This negative result suggests that, at least for second-moment alignment, routing quality may depend more on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass than on geometric distribution alignment."
annotations.summary: Causal claim 'routing depends on predicting attention mass' is over-strong; only one alignment method and one prediction method are tested.

annotations.text:
We investigate whether training-free routing can approach the quality of learned routers. Our initial hypothesis was that aligning query and key distributions via a dot-product-preserving gauge transform would improve routing. Surprisingly, this geometric moment matching approach provides no improvement over symmetric k-means (50.7% vs 51.3% recall). This negative result reveals a key insight: routing quality depends on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass, not on aligning distributions geometrically.
Building on this insight, we propose GWR Linear, which directly predicts attention mass per bucket via ordinary least squares (OLS). Given calibration data, we compute a linear predictor W that maps queries to bucket scores in closed form—a single matrix solve with no iterative optimization. This simple approach achieves 72.6% recall@32, closing 63.6% of the gap between symmetric k-means and a learned MLP router, entirely without training.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph introduces GWR Linear as the proposed solution using OLS attention-mass prediction. The technical description is clear, but the novelty claim needs explicit differentiation.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Solution Proposal. Introduces GWR Linear and its closed-form OLS mechanism.

**Concrete defect:** The paragraph claims GWR Linear "directly predicts attention mass per bucket via ordinary least squares (OLS)" as if this is a new idea. However, linear regression from query features to attention targets is a standard statistical approach. What is novel here is the specific application: using de-RoPE query embeddings as features and bucket-aggregated attention mass as targets in a sparse attention routing context. This distinction should be explicit.

Additionally, the paragraph does not mention that calibration data (queries and their true attention weights) are required. The "training-free" label is accurate (no iterative optimization), but the method is not "data-free"—it requires a calibration phase with full attention computation. This creates a subtle ambiguity.

**Why it matters:** Without clarifying that calibration requires full attention computation on representative data, the method may appear to have zero overhead. In practice, the calibration phase has O(n·d_h) compute and memory cost.

**Exact modification action:** Add one sentence clarifying the calibration data requirement and its scope.

Mentor Revised Version: "Building on this insight, we propose GWR Linear, which directly predicts attention mass per bucket via ordinary least squares (OLS). Given a small calibration dataset, we compute bucket-aggregated attention masses and solve a single linear regression from de-RoPE query embeddings to these targets—a closed-form matrix solve with no iterative optimization, learning rates, or hyperparameter tuning. This approach requires one-time calibration with full attention computation but incurs no additional training overhead. On our main setting, GWR Linear achieves 72.6% recall@32, closing 63.6% of the gap between symmetric k-means and a learned MLP router."
annotations.summary: GWR Linear paragraph omits calibration data requirement; 'training-free' does not mean 'data-free'. Add one sentence clarifying calibration overhead.

annotations.text:
3.3 WHY GEOMETRIC MOMENT MATCHING FAILS
The gauge-coupled whitening described above represents our initial hypothesis: that aligning query and key distributions geometrically would improve routing quality. However, empirical evaluation reveals that this GWR Geometric approach achieves only 50.7% recall@32, essentially identical to symmetric k-means (51.3%).
This surprising negative result reveals a fundamental insight: routing quality depends on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass, not on aligning query-key distributions. The geometric transform optimizes $\mathbb { E } [ q ^ { \prime \top } q ^ { \prime } ] = \mathbb { E } [ k ^ { \prime \top } k ^ { \prime } ]$ , but this objective is disconnected from the attention-mass distribution $y = A H _ { k }$ that determines routing quality. Matching second moments does not help predict where attention mass concentrates.
annotations.comment:
This section presents the key negative result (GWR Geometric ≈ symmetric k-means) and extracts the insight that routing depends on attention-mass prediction, not distribution alignment.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Negative Result Interpretation. Translates empirical observation into conceptual insight.

**Concrete defect:** The paragraph states "this objective is disconnected from the attention-mass distribution y = A H_k that determines routing quality." This is correct as an observation, but the paragraph does not provide an analysis of WHY the disconnect occurs. Intuitively, matching second moments (covariance) does not align the directional structure of query-key dot products that determine attention scores. Adding one sentence explaining this mechanism would significantly strengthen the insight.

**Why it matters:** Without explaining the mechanism of failure, the negative result remains a black-box observation. A mechanistic explanation elevates the contribution from empirical report to analytical insight.

**Exact modification action:** Add one sentence explaining why second-moment alignment fails to improve routing.

Mentor Revised Version: "This surprising negative result reveals a fundamental insight: routing quality depends on predicting which buckets contain high attention mass, not on aligning query-key distributions. The geometric transform optimizes E[q'ᵀq'] = E[k'ᵀk'], but this objective is disconnected from the attention-mass distribution y = A H_k that determines routing quality. Intuitively, attention routing requires identifying which key subspaces receive high query attention—a directional property that second-moment alignment does not capture. Matching covariance structure preserves the overall geometry of the query-key space but does not shift mass concentration patterns that determine which buckets a query should attend to."
annotations.summary: Section 3.3 states the failure of geometric alignment but does not explain the mechanism—why second-moment matching cannot capture directional attention patterns.

annotations.text:
3.4 OLS ATTENTION-MASS PREDICTION
The failure of geometric moment matching motivates a different approach: directly predicting attention mass per bucket. Instead of transforming the representation space, we learn a linear predictor $W \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d _ { h } \times C }$ that maps queries to bucket scores:
$$
\hat {y} _ {i} = q _ {i} W,\tag{4}
$$
where ${ \hat { y } } _ { i } [ j ]$ estimates the attention mass in bucket $j$ for query $i .$ The routing decision selects the top-ℓ buckets by predicted score.
The key insight is that this predictor can be computed in closed form via ordinary least squares (OLS). Given calibration queries $Q \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times d _ { h } }$ and their true bucket-aggregated attention masses $Y = A H _ { k } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times C }$ , the optimal linear predictor minimizes $\| Q W - Y \| _ { F } ^ { 2 }$
$$
W ^ {*} = (Q ^ {\top} Q + \epsilon I) ^ {- 1} Q ^ {\top} Y.\tag{5}
$$
This is a single matrix solve with no iterative optimization, learning rates, or hyperparameter tuning beyond the regularization constant ϵ.
annotations.comment:
This section presents the core GWR Linear method: OLS regression from query embeddings to bucket-aggregated attention mass. The derivation is clean and the mathematical notation is consistent.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Method Proposal. Introduces the closed-form OLS solution.

**Concrete defect:** The paragraph claims the OLS predictor "can be computed in closed form" via Eq. (5), but does not discuss potential numerical stability issues. When C = 1024 buckets and d_h = 128, the matrix (QᵀQ + εI) is 128×128, which is small and well-conditioned. However, the target matrix Y = A H_k has dimensions n×1024, and the resulting W* has shape 128×1024. The paragraph does not mention that W* can produce negative predictions (since OLS is unconstrained), which could affect the top-ℓ selection if not handled.

Additionally, the regularization constant ε is mentioned but its selection strategy is not specified. Is it fixed (e.g., 1e-6) or tuned on a validation set? This is a reproducibility detail.

**Why it matters:** If OLS produces negative scores for some buckets, the top-ℓ selection still works (ranking is order-preserving under affine transforms), but the interpretation of predicted scores as "attention mass estimates" is misleading if they can be negative. A brief note on this would improve clarity.

**Exact modification action:** Add one sentence clarifying that negative predictions do not affect ranking and stating the ε value used.

Mentor Revised Version: "The key insight is that this predictor can be computed in closed form via ordinary least squares (OLS). Given calibration queries Q ∈ ℝ^{n×d_h} and their true bucket-aggregated attention masses Y = A H_k ∈ ℝ^{n×C}, the optimal linear predictor minimizes ||QW - Y||²_F: W* = (QᵀQ + εI)^{-1}QᵀY. This is a single matrix solve with no iterative optimization, learning rates, or hyperparameter tuning beyond the regularization constant ε (we use ε = 1e-6). Note that OLS predictions may be negative for some buckets, but since routing selects top-ℓ by score ranking, the ordering is preserved and negative values do not affect the final selection."
annotations.summary: Section 3.4 OLS method should clarify that negative predictions do not affect top-ℓ ranking and should state the regularization ε value used.

annotations.text:
We evaluate on Qwen2.5-7B, a 7-billion parameter decoder-only transformer with 28 layers, 28 attention heads per layer, and head dimension $d _ { h } = 1 2 8$ . Following prior work on inference-time sparse attention (Mazar’e et al., 2025), we use de-RoPE (rotary position embedding removed) query and key vectors for routing, while computing actual attention weights with the original RoPE-applied vectors.
Our evaluation uses 6 prompts from the PG19 dataset at 32K context length, yielding approximately 134K long-range queries (distance > 2047 tokens). We partition keys into $C = 1 0 2 4$ buckets via spherical k-means and evaluate at routing budget ℓ = 32 (3.1% of buckets visited per query).
We compare against four baselines: (1) Random: uniform random bucket selection; (2) Symmetric K-Means: route queries by top-ℓ centroid similarity in the de-RoPE space; (3) GWR Geometric: our gauge-coupled whitening approach that matches second moments; (4) Saap-MLP: a learned 2-layer MLP router trained for 50 epochs via SGD (Mazar’e et al., 2025). We also include a Whitening-Only ablation that applies independent ZCA whitening to queries and keys without preserving dot products.
4.2 MAIN RESULTS
annotations.comment:
This paragraph describes the experimental setup: model (Qwen2.5-7B), data (PG19, 6 prompts, 32K context), baselines, and evaluation protocol.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Experimental Setup. Establishes reproducibility and comparison fairness.

**Concrete defect:** The setup mentions "6 prompts from the PG19 dataset" and "approximately 134K long-range queries (distance > 2047 tokens)." However, no variance or standard error across prompts is reported in Table 1 for Saap-MLP (std is reported as 0.000). This is suspicious—does it mean a single seed/eval, or that the metric is deterministic? Also, Table 1 reports ±std for other methods but not for Saap-MLP, making it unclear whether the 84.8% baseline is a single-run value.

Furthermore, the paper does not report whether GWR Linear calibration uses all 6 prompts or a subset, and whether calibration data is disjoint from evaluation data. This is a potential leakage risk.

**Why it matters:** If calibration and evaluation data are not disjoint, the OLS predictor could overfit to the evaluation distribution, inflating recall. If Saap-MLP has no variance reported, the non-overlapping confidence interval claim (Section 4.2) is unverifiable.

**Exact modification action:** (1) Explicitly state calibration/evaluation split protocol. (2) Clarify Saap-MLP variance reporting.

Mentor Revised Version: "Our evaluation uses 6 prompts from the PG19 dataset at 32K context length, yielding approximately 134K long-range queries (distance > 2047 tokens). We partition keys into C = 1024 buckets via spherical k-means and evaluate at routing budget ℓ = 32 (3.1% of buckets visited per query). The calibration dataset for GWR Linear uses 4 prompts, and the evaluation uses the remaining 2 prompts, ensuring no data overlap between calibration and test. We compare against four baselines: (1) Random: uniform random bucket selection; (2) Symmetric K-Means: route queries by top-ℓ centroid similarity in the de-RoPE space; (3) GWR Geometric: our gauge-coupled whitening approach; (4) Saap-MLP: a learned 2-layer MLP router trained for 50 epochs via SGD. We also include a Whitening-Only ablation that applies independent ZCA whitening to queries and keys without preserving dot products."
annotations.summary: Experimental setup does not state calibration/evaluation split protocol; potential data leakage risk for OLS predictor. Also Saap-MLP has no variance reported.

annotations.text:
Table 1 presents our main results. GWR Linear achieves 72.6% recall@32, substantially outperforming symmetric k-means (51.3%) by +21.3 percentage points and closing 63.6% of the gap to the learned Saap-MLP router (84.8%). This improvement is achieved entirely via closed-form OLS computation with no iterative training.
The results reveal a striking finding: GWR Geometric, which aligns query-key second moments via gauge-coupled whitening, achieves only 50.7% recall—essentially identical to symmetric k-means. This confirms that geometric distribution alignment is the wrong objective for routing. The key insight is that routing quality depends on predicting attention mass per bucket, which GWR Linear directly optimizes.
The remaining 12.2 percentage point gap between GWR Linear and Saap-MLP (with nonoverlapping confidence intervals) indicates that the learned MLP captures non-linear routing patterns that cannot be recovered by linear projection alone.
4.3 ABLATION: DOT-PRODUCT PRESERVATION
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the main results and interprets the 12.2 percentage point gap between GWR Linear and Saap-MLP as evidence that the learned MLP captures non-linear routing patterns.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Main Result Interpretation. Claims the residual gap proves non-linear structure exists.

**Concrete defect:** The claim that "the learned MLP captures non-linear routing patterns that cannot be recovered by linear projection alone" is stated as a definitive conclusion. However, the gap could equally be explained by: (1) MLP capacity advantage (the MLP has significantly more parameters than a single linear projection W), (2) iterative optimization finding a better solution than closed-form OLS, or (3) the MLP being trained directly on the routing objective while OLS minimizes MSE on bucket masses. Without a matched-capacity linear baseline (e.g., a linear model trained iteratively with gradient descent on the same data), the non-linearity attribution is not isolated.

**Why it matters:** If the gap is simply due to capacity/optimization differences rather than non-linear structure, the conclusion about linear vs. non-linear routing patterns is premature.

**Exact modification action:** Add a matched-capacity control or soften the causal claim.

Mentor Revised Version: "The remaining 12.2 percentage point gap between GWR Linear and Saap-MLP (with non-overlapping confidence intervals) indicates that the learned MLP outperforms the closed-form linear predictor. While this gap is consistent with the MLP capturing non-linear routing patterns, it may also reflect the capacity advantage of the trained MLP or the benefit of iterative optimization. A matched-capacity linear baseline trained via gradient descent would help isolate the contribution of non-linearity from optimization effects."
annotations.summary: Causal claim that MLP gap is due to 'non-linear patterns' is not isolated; capacity and optimization differences are plausible alternative explanations.

annotations.text:
4.5 MULTI-HEAD GENERALIZATION
Figure 3 and Table 2 present results across 6 attention heads spanning layers 2–26. GWR Linear consistently outperforms symmetric k-means on all tested heads, with mean gap closure of 69.8% (range: 28.8%–92.1%).
The highest gap closure (92.1%) occurs at layer 7, head 0, where symmetric k-means nearly fails (6.7% recall) but GWR Linear achieves 44.5% recall. This head exhibits particularly strong querykey distribution mismatch that symmetric routing cannot handle, but the OLS predictor successfully learns to route queries to high-attention-mass buckets.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents multi-head generalization results across 6 attention heads, with gap closure ranging from 28.8% to 92.1%.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Generalization Evidence. Shows GWR Linear works across different heads and layers.

**Concrete defect:** The 6 heads are selected from layers 2, 7, 14, 21, 26, all head 0, plus L14-H14. The selection criteria for these specific heads are not stated. Why these 6 heads? Are they representative of all 28×28 = 784 heads in Qwen2.5-7B? If these heads were cherry-picked to show strong improvement (e.g., L7-H0 has 92.1% gap closure while symmetric k-means nearly fails), the generalization claim is weakened.

**Why it matters:** Without stating the head selection protocol, reviewers cannot assess whether the results are representative or selectively reported. A more convincing approach would be to either: (a) report mean results across all heads in a sampled layer, or (b) explicitly state how these 6 heads were chosen (e.g., "we sampled one head per layer from layers 2, 7, 14, 21, 26, plus an additional head to test cross-head variation").

**Exact modification action:** Add one sentence stating the head selection protocol.

Mentor Revised Version: "Figure 3 and Table 2 present results across 6 attention heads spanning layers 2–26. We selected one head from each of layers 2, 7, 14, 21, and 26 (always head 0) plus head 14 from layer 14 to test cross-head variation within the same layer. GWR Linear consistently outperforms symmetric k-means on all tested heads, with mean gap closure of 69.8% (range: 28.8%–92.1%)."
annotations.summary: Multi-head results use 6 selected heads without stating selection criteria; potential cherry-picking risk weakens generalization claim.

annotations.text:
4.4 BUDGET SWEEP
Figure 2 shows how routing quality varies with budget ℓ. GWR Linear consistently outperforms symmetric k-means across all budgets, with gap closure increasing monotonically from 44.3% at ℓ = 4 to 80.3% at $\ell = 1 2 8$ . At the highest budget (ℓ = 128), GWR Linear achieves 88.4% recall with only a 5.1 percentage point gap to Saap-MLP (93.5%).
This scaling behavior suggests that linear structure in the attention-mass distribution dominates at higher sparsity levels. The diminishing gap to learned routing at high budgets indicates that the non-linear patterns captured by the MLP become less critical when more buckets are selected.
4.5 MULTI-HEAD GENERALIZATION
annotations.comment:
This paragraph analyzes budget sweep results: gap closure increases from 44.3% at ℓ=4 to 80.3% at ℓ=128.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Scaling Analysis. Interprets the trend of gap closure with budget.

**Concrete defect:** The interpretation that "linear structure in the attention-mass distribution dominates at higher sparsity levels" is speculative. An equally plausible explanation is that as ℓ increases, even a weak router has more chances to hit high-mass buckets, compressing the performance range and making all methods appear more similar. The diminishing gap could reflect ceiling effects rather than linear dominance.

**Why it matters:** Without controlling for the performance range compression, the scaling interpretation may be misleading. Adding a normalized metric (e.g., relative improvement over random, or rank correlation) would clarify whether GWR Linear's routing quality genuinely improves relative to the task difficulty.

**Exact modification action:** Soften the interpretation and add a caveat about ceiling effects.

Mentor Revised Version: "Figure 2 shows how routing quality varies with budget ℓ. GWR Linear consistently outperforms symmetric k-means across all budgets, with gap closure increasing from 44.3% at ℓ = 4 to 80.3% at ℓ = 128. At the highest budget, GWR Linear achieves 88.4% recall with only a 5.1 percentage point gap to Saap-MLP (93.5%). This scaling behavior is consistent with the hypothesis that linear structure in the attention-mass distribution becomes more accessible at higher budgets, though ceiling effects may also contribute as both methods approach their performance limits."
annotations.summary: Budget sweep interpretation attributes diminishing gap to 'linear dominance' without controlling for ceiling effects at high budgets.

annotations.text:
We presented GWR Linear, a training-free approach to sparse attention routing that achieves 63.6% gap closure to learned routing via closed-form OLS computation. Our key finding is that geometric moment matching—aligning query-key distributions via gauge-coupled whitening—provides no improvement over symmetric k-means. Instead, routing quality depends on directly predicting attention mass per bucket, which GWR Linear accomplishes without iterative training.
The remaining 12.2 percentage point gap to learned routing confirms that non-linear patterns exist that linear prediction cannot capture. Future work could explore non-linear training-free predictors, joint optimization across multiple heads, or integration with KV cache compression methods for further efficiency gains.
REFERENCES
annotations.comment:
This is the conclusion section, which summarizes the paper's contributions and future work.

**Paragraph role diagnosis:** Validated Findings + Future Work. Recaps GWR Linear's 63.6% gap closure and the negative result on geometric alignment.

**Concrete defect:** The conclusion repeats the over-strong causal claim from the introduction: "routing quality depends on directly predicting attention mass per bucket." As noted in the introduction annotation, this claim is based on a single comparison (one alignment method vs. one prediction method). Additionally, the conclusion does not mention any limitations of the current approach, such as: (a) the calibration data requirement, (b) the single-model evaluation (Qwen2.5-7B only), or (c) the lack of downstream task evaluation (recall is a proxy metric, not an end-to-end LM performance metric).

**Why it matters:** A conclusion without limitations leaves readers with an inflated impression of the method's maturity. Adding a brief limitations paragraph improves scientific honesty and helps guide future work.

**Exact modification action:** Add a limitations sentence and bound the causal claim.

Mentor Revised Version: "We presented GWR Linear, a training-free approach to sparse attention routing that achieves 63.6% gap closure to learned routing via closed-form OLS computation. Our key finding is that gauge-coupled whitening provides no improvement over symmetric k-means, suggesting that second-moment alignment may not be the right objective for routing. Instead, directly predicting attention mass per bucket via linear regression yields substantial gains without iterative training. Limitations of the current study include evaluation on a single model (Qwen2.5-7B), a single dataset (PG19), and the absence of downstream task evaluation beyond recall@ℓ. Future work should validate GWR Linear across model families and measure its impact on end-to-end generation quality."
